properties.decision:
Recorded as BRAINSTORMING, not as a proposal — a twist on dec:idea-does-a-growing-ruleset-converge-or-bloom-and-can-any-design-be-assured-of-closure. Anthony, 2026-09-06, in his words: "at a certain point, the design becomes so cemented in that adding anything new or altering a design becomes very challenging. I learned this in my ophyd-service project exploration project. as I kept trying to say, I don't want this anymore, I found that I had to start reversing requirement after requirement. I had gone so far back that at a certain point, I just decided it would be better/easier to start a new (unrelated to ophyd-service) rather than continuing to unravel or peel back accepted decision after accepted decision. hence, I created qs project as a completely new design. I feel that we are way past this point now in reflow2 that if I wanted to completely overhaul some aspect of reflow2, it would be easier to start a new design rather than peel back probably hundreds of decisions that have got us to this point. basically, the core aspects of reflow2 design are probably cemented into the design. now we are only focusing on the edges/perimeter of the design. after a time, this will also become cemented in if the design continues to bloom outward."

WHAT THE GRAPH SAYS ABOUT THE OPHYD-SERVICE CASE (fact:the-fork-ask-is-a-deferred-branch-whose-reopening-condition-is-now-met, 2026-08-31): what that project needed was a BRANCH AT A DECISION with the health machinery still working — world-scoped alternatives inside one graph — and dec:parallel-alternatives had deferred exactly that until field evidence arrived. Starting qs as a new design was the workaround for a missing primitive, not only a verdict on the old design.

THE FRAMINGS, as they separate (none is a decision):

(a) CEMENT IS MEASURABLE, AND IT IS NOT WHERE THE FEELING PUTS IT. A k-core decomposition of this design over design edges only (release manifests, snapshots, epochs and acknowledgement bookkeeping excluded) has a maximum shell of k=5 holding 93 nodes: 37 ChangeEvents, 28 Artifacts, 17 Components, 6 Capabilities, 5 Interfaces — the schema files, the core modules (detect, graph, heal, report, nodes, schema) and the components they realize. ACCEPTED DECISIONS ARE NOT IN THE CORE: 172 of 175 accepted Decisions on the design graph sit at k≤3, none at k≥10. Structurally, what is cemented is the VOCABULARY and the code that realizes it; the decisions govern from the perimeter. Counter-argument: the feeling of "hundreds of decisions to peel back" is real and the edges do not show it because decisions cement through their PROSE — "distinct from X, which decided Y" — which is the same finding as the sibling brainstorm: the forks are not drawn, so the interlock is invisible to any graph operation.

(b) PACE LAYERING (Brand's shearing layers; Alexander's unfolding). A built thing has layers that change at different rates, and a slow core is what makes it a design rather than a pile. On this reading cementing is not a pathology; the pathology is an UNDECLARED layer — a decision that everyone treats as foundation with nothing saying so. Counter-argument: reflow2 has no vocabulary for "this is the slow layer"; the closest is k-shell depth, computed rather than stated, and Anthony's own SE background (viewpoints, baselines) says a baseline is DECLARED, not inferred.

(c) THE COST OF REVERSAL IS COMPUTABLE PER DECISION. propagate_change from a Decision gives its blast radius; the downstream closure of an accepted Decision is its reversal cost; a report ranking accepted Decisions by that cost would name the load-bearing ones before anyone tries to move them. Counter-argument: the earlier optimize work found the propagation costs ~5 s per scan on this graph, so a per-decision sweep over 367 accepted Decisions is a batch job, not an orientation call.

(d) STARTING OVER DISCARDS EXACTLY THE DECISIONS, AND THAT WAS MEASURED. dec:idea-genesis-reflow3-from-the-requirements-alone asked whether genesis on reflow2's own requirements would rebuild reflow2, and measured NO: the gap is 18 capabilities and 389 decisions. A restart from intent keeps the requirements and loses the reasoning. Counter-argument: sometimes losing the reasoning is the point — qs was cheap to start because its INTENT differed from ophyd-service's, so the discarded decisions were for a system nobody wanted any more; the cost is only a cost when the intent survives.

(e) REVERSAL IS PRACTISED HERE, NOT IMPOSSIBLE. Measured: 367 accepted Decisions, 12 superseded, 4 rejected; 42 OBSOLETES edges (12 onto Decisions, 15 onto Artifacts, 5 onto Interfaces); Requirements 144 accepted, 9 dropped, 4 deferred. Roughly 4–7% of accepted intent has been reversed in seven weeks, on the record, without a restart. Counter-argument: those are perimeter reversals; nothing in the core (the schema, the coherence loop, the store) has been reversed, which is Anthony's point — and whether that is because it is right or because it is cemented cannot be told from the count.

(f) THE PERIMETER-CEMENTS-TOO PREDICTION IS TESTABLE. Every node added in this session sits at k=3 (the new rule, the new capability): the design is blooming outward. The prediction says new nodes will start landing at high k. That is one number per release — the k-shell distribution of nodes added since the last cut — and it would say whether the perimeter is thickening into core. Counter-argument: k-core is a structural proxy; a decision can be socially cemented (everyone builds on it) while structurally peripheral, and the proxy will miss that.

WHAT IS CHEAP: (a), (e) and (f) are one-line measurements on the export and were taken above. (c) is a batch report. WHAT IS EXPENSIVE: world-scoped alternatives (d)-adjacent, the deferred primitive ophyd-service needed, which dec:parallel-alternatives judged a large invasive change.
properties.name: OPEN — does a design cement from the core outward until unwinding accepted decisions costs more than starting a new design? Is reflow2 past that point, and will its perimeter cement too?
properties.rationale: A RANKING IS A FINDING, NOT A DECISION. The measurement disagrees with the feeling in a useful way: the cement is the schema and the core modules (k=5 shell, 93 nodes), and accepted decisions sit on the perimeter (172 of 175 at k≤3) — so "peel back hundreds of decisions" is a cost carried in prose, not in edges, which is the same missing-fork-edge finding the sibling brainstorm reached from the other direction. Two things follow without deciding anything. First, the honest name for "we are past the point of overhaul" is a DECLARED BASELINE — Anthony's own SE vocabulary — and reflow2 cannot say it today except by computing a k-shell. Second, the ophyd-service lesson as the graph holds it is not "designs cement" but "the primitive for exploring an alternative inside a live design was deferred until field evidence arrived, and it has arrived" — starting qs was the workaround. Whether the core SHOULD be revisable is a different question from whether it CAN be, and only the second one is measurable. Nothing here is proposed for building; the one cheap instrument is the per-release k-shell distribution of new nodes (f), and the one expensive thing is the deferred world-scoping that dec:parallel-alternatives already owns. Anthony's call.
